articles.title: New home for orangutans rescued from Indonesia's burning forests
articles.dek: Deep in a forest in Indonesian Borneo, conservationists open a cage.
paragraphs: Deep in a forest in Indonesian Borneo, conservationists open a cage. A female orangutan and her baby waste little time, clambering up the towering trees and disappearing into the canopy, safe at last.
The pair were among nine orangutans rescued from devastating wildfires ravaging their forest home in Ketapang, West Kalimantan province, in August and September.
Nursed back to health over several weeks, they now have a new home in Batu Nyambu, a 23,000-hectare (56,800-acre) protected area in the same province.
When they were rescued, the animals were in bad shape, YIARI wildlife rehabilitation foundation CEO Karmele Llano Sanchez told AFP journalists who went along for the release.
"Some of them had burns on their hands and feet, and some of them were skinny and malnourished," said Sanchez.
"They had to be cared for and fed until they were in good condition again."

The journey to get them to their new home was long and arduous, with conservation workers trekking for hours through steep, slippery terrain, carrying the orangutans in cages suspended from poles digging into their shoulders.
Conservationists clapped in joy as the apes fled the cages on Thursday and returned to the wild where they belong.
Among the nine orangutans were four pairs of mothers and their young.
Sanchez said three of the mothers were pregnant again—a fact discovered during the final health check before their release.
One of those expecting is Mama Ocha, who was rescued along with her baby, Ocha.
"The team will stay around to make sure that she is all right and that she can deliver her baby, and that will be an excellent outcome," said Sanchez.
Once widespread across Southeast Asia, orangutans are now critically endangered.
According to conservation group WWF, only around 104,000 remain in the wild in Borneo and Sumatra, less than half the estimated population a century ago.

articles.title: For many, striped bass fishing is a way of life. But the iconic species could face collapse
articles.dek: Striped bass fishing has been Bill Jakob's passion for more than 60 years, and he remembers an era when he'd spend all night casting his line into the crashing waves off…
paragraphs: Striped bass fishing has been Bill Jakob's passion for more than 60 years, and he remembers an era when he'd spend all night casting his line into the crashing waves off Montauk and get eight or nine fish ranging up to 40 pounds (18 kilograms), a big catch by anyone's standards.
Then, after years of heavy fishing, the big runs of stripers stopped.

"I'm part of the problem, back in the years. I ran party boats, we slayed fish with reckless abandon," said Jakob, president of the Montauk Surfcasters Association on the easternmost tip of Long Island.
Increasingly, fishermen like Jakob fear the good days of catching striped bass are coming to an end. The fish aren't showing up like they used to, and young stripers are becoming harder to find.

Scientists who study striped bass say anglers on the East Coast are right to be concerned, and they say years of overfishing are just part of the problem. The fish have experienced eight consecutive years of poor reproduction in their most critical habitat in the Chesapeake Bay, regulators said last week, and the population has declined along much of the Atlantic coast.

Factors like years of warming waters—a prime concern cited by many scientists—poor river flow, drought, pollution and possibly increased predation from seals and sharks have left experts and fishermen asking whether tighter fishing limits would even be enough for striped bass to recover. Losing these higher-level predators, which help regulate smaller fish, would threaten an $8 billion fishing industry and tens of thousands of jobs.

"Stripers" are prized in part because they put up a fight and can be fished right from shore. From the slippery rocks of Maine's coast to the warmer waters of the St. Johns River in Florida, anglers wearing headlamps can be seen casting into the predawn darkness, hoping for a bite.

Interstate regulators have made changes to the way the migratory fish are managed in recent years, including standardizing the way they're measured against size requirements. But regulators have balked at reducing the level of recreational catch. Some fishermen say the current moves might not go far enough, and stricter action—including possibly a fishing moratorium, a strategy used in the 1980s—is needed to ensure that future generations of anglers can still catch striped bass.

"They are not replacing themselves at a sufficient level. That obviously has everybody concerned," said Beth Versak, the striped bass program manager for the Maryland Department of Natural Resources. "People all up and down the coast are passionate about striped bass."
Fishing guides, boat trips, gear, bait, hotel rooms—it all adds up to what members of the industry say is about $8 billion in economic impact and as many as 100,000 jobs in the U. S. alone.

"Striped bass as we know it is going to collapse," said Patrick Paquette, government affairs coordinator for the Massachusetts Striped Bass Association and a member of an interstate advisory panel about the regulations.
"Sometime around 2029, 2030 it's going to go off a cliff," he said, "and it's going to be ugly."

Striped bass hatch in fresh or brackish water and then spend the early years of their lives in estuaries where the rivers meet the sea. Their ability to reproduce and bring new fish into the population is predicated on environmental conditions that favor them—specifically, cool, wet springs.

Scientists identify four major spawning stocks along the Atlantic. The Chesapeake Bay is where up to 90% of stripers spawn and grow. When freshwater flows are too low, such as in times of drought, or when spring or summer temperatures are too high, the fish suffer and populations can fall, said Toni Kerns, fisheries policy director with the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, which regulates striped bass.

articles.title: Chemists create disappearing tattoos: Here's the science behind how they work
articles.dek: How handy would it be if you could make your tattoos invisible for a job interview in the morning, and reveal them again for a party in the evening?
paragraphs: How handy would it be if you could make your tattoos invisible for a job interview in the morning, and reveal them again for a party in the evening? This sounds like science fiction, but it may soon be reality.

Researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder have developed invisible tattoo ink that can be revealed with a UV flashlight and stays visible until switched off with white light. They have published their research in the journal Matter & Light .
They created different motifs with this ink ranging from a lantern that reveals its light when activated, to multicolored scales like those in the much-loved children's book "The Rainbow Fish."

The pigments used in these inks are so-called photochromic dyes (from the Greek "photos," which means "light," and "chroma," which means "color"). In other words, they are compounds that change color when exposed to light. These dyes have been used for years in color-changing sunglasses.
Light carries energy, and photochromic compounds are designed in such a way that this energy is enough to cause a chemical change that alters the shape and therefore the properties of the molecule.

In the case of the "invisible" tattoo ink, two or three seconds of bright ultraviolet (UV) light is enough to form a new ring in the dye molecule, which switches a colorless pigment to a colored one. A variety of colors are available depending on the exact structure of the molecule.

A blast of bright white light reverses the reaction, breaking the ring and turning the color off again. For a long time, the challenge with this chemistry was that the colored form of the dye was relatively unstable and quickly reverted to the more stable, colorless form—especially at higher temperatures.

Another issue was fatigue: after a certain number of on-off cycles, the dyes degraded and took on a permanent colored hue. Have you ever bought transition lens sunglasses and noticed that they became less effective over time? This is due to the same deterioration of photochromic compounds in the lenses. But thanks to recent research efforts, remarkably stable dyes have been designed that reliably hold their color for months and can undergo over 10,000 activation and deactivation cycles without degrading.

Carson Bruns' team at the University of Colorado Boulder showed that these pigments could be formulated into tattoo inks by encapsulating them in poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) , a polymer approved for medical use in bone cement, dentures and intraocular lenses. This family of inks is known as PhotoTat.

So, when will you be able to get one of these switchable tattoos? A red pigment was already launched in 2024 under the name Magic Ink by Colorado-based biotech company Hyprskn . A 2-milliliter (ml) vial will set you back £77, which is about 100 times more expensive than regular tattoo ink due to the specialized dyes and formulation process required. The ink is fully compliant with the EU's Reach (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals) safety regulations.

Now, Bruns' research team has developed three more PhotoTat inks—blue, magenta and yellow—that can combine into 16 other colors. "So far," Bruns says , "the only person who's tested this ink is me. I actually have hundreds of these tattoos on my legs now and they've all gone really well."

Some challenges remain, though: direct sunlight contains enough UV radiation to activate the tattoos unless they are protected by sunscreen. Indoor light will slowly switch them off over a period of several days.

In addition, the blue ink currently degrades after only 10–100 activations , leaving a permanent, purple-colored mark. Most importantly, the inks need to undergo thorough toxicity and safety testing before they can be rolled out to tattoo shops for general use, which will likely take several years. Don't get your hopes up just yet about your new "business during the day, party at night" look.

When Hyprskn launched Magic Ink, the reception in the tattoo community was mixed. While some tattoo enthusiasts viewed it as a revolutionary creative tool, others thought it was an overpriced gimmick. Bruns does not only see his photochromic tattoo inks as fashion accessories, however.

articles.title: Are narcissists multiplying or is the social media algorithm making them bolder? The answer in five stages
articles.dek: Social media doesn't necessarily reflect who you are, but it may intensify particular personality traits and confirm or even persuade you that your worst behavior is justified.
paragraphs: Social media doesn't necessarily reflect who you are, but it may intensify particular personality traits and confirm or even persuade you that your worst behavior is justified.
We are addressing that imbalance with our framework, the Algorithmic Trait Amplification, or ATA, with particular regard to narcissism.

Narcissism runs on a spectrum . At the far end is narcissistic personality disorder, a clinical diagnosis. But many people have milder narcissistic traits—a strong need for admiration, a habit of overrating their own importance, difficulty taking criticism, little empathy. That said, some traits such as healthy ambition and assertiveness are beneficial.
People who have these traits , which are common, are especially drawn to social media and platforms built around status and approval from others.

For years we have been studying online behavior and the effect of social media on relationships , including how psychopathy shows up in romantic relationships and how TikTok shapes young women's attraction to dangerous partners .

That work, combined with what psychology already knows on how narcissistic people operate online , how algorithms chase engagement and what personality change requires , led us to a realization. The algorithmic loop process may slowly strengthen an inflated, entitled self-image.
These are the five steps over which ATA predicts that social media will heighten narcissistic traits.

Someone with narcissistic traits tends to react strongly to content that matches their self-image. Winning. Status. Being special. Always being right. Most of us have some version of a For You content feed. But for people high in these traits, the pull is more powerful. Such content fulfills a narcissist's higher need for validation.

Social media recommendation systems are designed to keep us engaged, but they cannot tell whether the content is good for us. They only measure whether it holds our attention. Our reactions become instructions : give this person more of this, feed the loop.

For example, a user rewatches a video about how "strong personalities intimidate weak people." The app notices and fills the feed with content about cutting off "toxic" friends and refusing to apologize. Every video tells them the problem is everyone else. And they agree. So, they watch more.

Audit studies of online recommendation systems show that feeds narrow in proportion to how selectively a user engages. Someone low in narcissistic traits engages more evenly in different types of content. Someone high in these traits engages hard and narrow, and the algorithm obliges.

We call this the echo algorithm, after the Greek myth of Narcissus . The nymph Echo can only repeat what is said to her. She cannot challenge or answer back.

Social media algorithms are the same. Over time, the user unknowingly builds a mirror: more praise, more validation, more self-image inflation. And the worst part for narcissistic users is that the feed feels like the world agrees with them. Objective. External. Almost all-knowing. But it is an oracle that they trained themselves to say exactly what they wanted to hear.

articles.title: Hidden erosion: Study reveals soft mountain rock erodes three times faster than hard rock—with climate implications
articles.dek: A University of Massachusetts Amherst-led research team has discovered that weaker rock in mountain landscapes erodes three times faster than harder rock—even on gentler…
paragraphs: A University of Massachusetts Amherst-led research team has discovered that weaker rock in mountain landscapes erodes three times faster than harder rock—even on gentler slopes—and is one of the main attributes governing mountain erosion. The finding also challenges our current understanding of the relationship between erosion and the release of carbon dioxide, and suggests that geologists and atmospheric scientists may be underestimating the CO₂ contributions coming from the Earth's rocky places.
The research, recently published in Science Advances , depends on a new technique relying on common quartz grains, the rare isotope beryllium-10 (known as ¹⁰Be) and cosmic rays from exploded stars.

Over the course of the universe's nearly 14 billion years, countless stars have exploded, and when they do, they blast out showers of cosmic shrapnel in the form of high-energy particles. These cosmic particles have been raining down on the Earth for uncountable ages at a constant rate. When the particles penetrate rocks on the surface, ¹⁰Be is produced within quartz. For four decades, geologists have been able to harvest these quartz grains from rocks like granite and sandstone, in which the quartz grains are comparatively large, to test all sorts of hypotheses.

But in rocks where the grains are too fine, such as shale, the conventional ¹⁰Be technique hasn't worked. And that has limited geologists' abilities to accurately pinpoint things like erosion rates across a broad spectrum of rock types.
That is, until Marder and his colleagues developed a new method for harvesting the rare isotope from such rocks.

"When we look at landscapes, we are only seeing a snapshot in time," says Eyal Marder, a postdoctoral researcher in earth, geographic and climate sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and the lead author of the new paper.

But researchers want to understand the full geological movie from start to finish in order to understand the land's life cycle. Marder and his team studied Colorado's East River Watershed, which drains approximately 465 square kilometers (180 square miles) of the southern Elk and West Elk mountains—jagged peaks whose most famous landmark, Crested Butte, is revered as one of the U. S.' s premier ski areas.
The sheer alpine topography is notable for its diverse geological composition: a mix of incredibly durable igneous rock and much weaker shale, deposited by rivers eons ago.

Their new technique allowed Marder and his team to make a few surprising discoveries. As expected, weaker sedimentary rocks erode faster than harder igneous ones. What was surprising is how much faster they erode.
"Shale's erodibility is three times that of the harder rocks in the East River Watershed," says Marder.

It's so fast that the contrast with the slower-eroding rocks can prolong landscape erosion over millions of years. This also means that the fastest erosion might happen not in steeper, more resistant parts of the mountains, but rather in lower, comparatively gentle, rounder, sedimentary ones.

This shift means that the best way to evaluate whether or not a landscape has reached equilibrium is not just by visually gauging its pitch, but also by estimating erosion rates from the amounts of ¹⁰Be in the sediment carried by the streams that drain mountainous regions.

Marder and his team have also exposed a missing piece in global climate models. Geologists recognize that weathering of different minerals on the surface can either release or absorb CO₂. But the fact that in mountainous landscapes, shale, which releases CO₂ to the atmosphere, is eroding faster and at a larger magnitude than intrusive rocks, which absorb CO₂ from the atmosphere, means that geologists and atmospheric scientists may have underestimated the CO₂ contributions coming from mountains.

"Scale our work up from the Elk and West Elk mountains to all the mountainous regions of the world, and getting erosion rates and their equivalent impact on CO₂ release right has a marked impact on what we know about biogeochemical global cycles and climate change," says Marder. "Give us the type of rock and enough quartz for our ¹⁰Be measurements, and we can estimate what effect it will have on CO₂ emissions from thousands to millions of years."

articles.title: Tiny photonic chip links telescopes together to view the universe in 'astonishing' detail
articles.dek: A tiny glass chip developed by researchers at Heriot-Watt University has linked two telescopes together to enable them to act as a single powerful instrument, marking an…
paragraphs: A tiny glass chip developed by researchers at Heriot-Watt University has linked two telescopes together to enable them to act as a single powerful instrument, marking an important step toward a new generation of astronomical technology.

The CHARA Array is one of the world's leading facilities for high-resolution astronomy and consists of six telescopes that can be linked together to study celestial objects in extraordinary detail. To make this possible, the light collected by each telescope must be combined with extreme precision.

The photonic chip—which guided light through thin glass channels in the manner of integrated circuits guiding electrons—has been successfully used for the first time in on-sky observations at the CHARA Array in California. The results show that the technology, small enough to fit in the palm of a hand, can perform a task that has traditionally required much larger and more complex optical systems.

The achievement could help transform the way future astronomical instruments are designed, making them smaller, more robust and easier to upgrade while still delivering the precision needed to study distant stars and planetary systems.
The study appears in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society .

Researchers believe the technology could eventually support some of astronomy's most ambitious goals, including studying how planetary systems form and evolve while helping scientists directly detect and characterize planets around other stars.

The international project brought together researchers from the U. K. (Heriot-Watt University), Germany (Cologne and Potsdam universities) and the United States (the CHARA Array of Georgia State University). The photonic chip at the heart of the instrument was developed at Heriot-Watt University's Institute of Photonics and Quantum Sciences by professor Robert Thomson and Dr. Aurélien Benoît. The team also played a central role in the observing campaigns that demonstrated the technology on the telescope array.

Thomson said, "This is a significant milestone for a research program that began more than 15 years ago. Astronomers can achieve much sharper views of the universe by combining observations from several telescopes at the same time. Doing this allows the telescopes to work together as though they were one much larger telescope.

"Traditionally, combining the light from multiple telescopes requires bulky instruments with complex arrangements of mirrors and lenses. We have shown that much of that work can instead be carried out by a glass chip only a couple of centimeters in size.

"Seeing this technology progress from fundamental research and early laboratory demonstrations to successful operation at one of the world's leading facilities is a particularly significant outcome and a demonstration of the power of international collaboration."

The Heriot-Watt photonic chip performs that role. Tiny channels are written directly using an ultrafast-laser inscription technique inside an innovative glass to provide access to an unexplored spectral range for this fabrication process. The channels combine the incoming light, enabling the separate telescopes to work together as a single telescope.

The chip sits at the heart of an instrument called CHARIOT, which was designed as a testbed for new photonic technologies. During observing campaigns in 2024 and 2025, CHARIOT successfully combined light from telescopes at the CHARA Array and recorded signals from a range of stars, demonstrating the precision required for advanced astronomical research. The instrument also detected signals from stars fainter than those reached by the system it replaced.

Benoît, from Heriot-Watt University's Institute of Photonics and Quantum Sciences, said, "There is something very special about seeing a device that we conceived, designed, fabricated and characterized in the laboratory being used to efficiently collect and analyze light from real stars at one of the world's leading astronomical interferometers.

articles.title: Zombies are real – just ask the parasites taking over the bodies and brains of insects and rodents, leading them to their doom
articles.dek: Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture. In Michael Jackson’s “ Thriller ” music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated…
paragraphs: Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture. In Michael Jackson’s “ Thriller ” music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated dance. In HBO’s “ The Last of Us ,” a fungus infects humans, takes over their bodies and turns them into hosts that help spread the infection. Even Plankton has tried his hand at taking control of another organism in “ SpongeBob SquarePants .”

These examples are fictional, but they all play with the same unsettling idea: Can one organism take control of another, even after they’re dead? In nature, the answer is not quite as dramatic, but some parasites and fungi come surprisingly close.

I spend much of my time as a biomedical engineer and synthetic biologist thinking about how biological systems sense signals, process information and change their behavior. That is part of what makes the idea of one organism taking control of another so fascinating to me.

Some parasites and fungi can alter the behavior of a living host in ways that benefit the parasite. They do not bring the dead back to life. Instead, they interfere with biological systems that control movement, motivation and decision-making.
The best-known example of a parasite changing its host’s behavior is the “zombie ant” fungus , Ophiocordyceps , which helped inspire “The Last of Us.”

The life cycle of the zombie ant fungus begins when fungal spores land on an ant. The spores stick to the ant’s outer surface and eventually break through it, allowing the fungus to enter the body. Once inside, the fungus grows and spreads while the ant is still alive. The infection can develop over several weeks before the most dramatic changes in the ant’s behavior begin.

Eventually, the infected ant leaves the colony and begins wandering and climbing vegetation. This behavior moves the ant away from its normal habitat and into a location that favors fungal reproduction and dispersal. Near the end of the infection, the ant bites tightly onto a leaf, twig or other plant surface and remains attached in what researchers call a death grip . After the ant dies, the fungus consumes the remaining tissues and produces a stalk from the ant’s body. This structure releases spores that can fall on other ants below and begin the cycle again.

How does the fungus make the ant do this? You might imagine fungal cells invading the ant’s brain and taking control. Surprisingly, researchers examining infected ants before death found extensive fungal growth throughout the body and around muscle fibers , but not inside the brain. Fungal cells can form networks around the ant’s muscles, suggesting that the ability to manipulate behavior may involve communication between the fungus and multiple host tissues rather than direct control of the brain.

The death grip provides an especially striking example of how the fungus can manipulate its host’s muscles. The jaw muscles of infected ants are heavily colonized by the fungus , showing signs of extreme contraction. There are also signs that the fungus may be releasing molecules near these tissues. Yet motor neurons and connections between nerves and muscles can remain intact. Together, these findings suggest that the fungus may alter the machinery controlling muscle contraction rather than simply destroying it.

Scientists still do not know exactly what causes ants to undergo the entire sequence of wandering, climbing and biting. While researchers have identified fungal genes associated with proteins, toxins and other compounds that could affect chemical signaling in the host, many of these possible mechanisms have not yet been proved.

That uncertainty is part of what makes the system so fascinating. The fungus does not appear to flip a single “zombie switch.” Instead, it may change several biological systems at once until the ant behaves in a way that benefits the fungus.
Ophiocordyceps is not the only organism capable of changing a host’s behavior.

The emerald jewel wasp, Ampulex compressa , uses a very different strategy: It injects venom into a cockroach’s nervous system. The cockroach is not paralyzed, but it becomes much less likely to start moving on its own or to escape. The wasp can then lead it to a burrow and lay an egg on it.

Researchers have shown that the venom reduces activity in parts of the nervous system involved in starting movement. In other words, the cockroach can still walk, but its drive to do so has been changed.

Hairworms take behavioral manipulation one step further by leading their hosts toward their own demise. Some species infect praying mantises or crickets and grow inside them while the insect is still alive. When the worm is ready to reproduce, the infected host becomes unusually attracted to light, which may draw it toward the shiny surface of water. The host enters the water, where the worm escapes from its body and begins the next stage of its life cycle. For the host that cannot swim, that behavior can be fatal.

Researchers are still working out exactly how the parasite causes this change, but studies have found changes in proteins in the host’s brain as the parasite manipulates it. In effect, the parasite appears to hijack the host’s sensory and behavioral machinery to guide it somewhere it would not normally go.
Behavioral manipulation also occurs in mammals. Toxoplasma gondii can infect many warm-blooded animals, but it reproduces in cats.

While rodents normally avoid cat odors, those infected with the parasite can lose some of that natural aversion and even become attracted to cat odors . This change could increase the chance that an infected rodent is eaten by a cat, allowing the parasite to complete its life cycle.

These examples show why “mind control” is an imperfect description of how parasites manipulate their hosts. Parasites do not need to control every action that their host makes. They may only need to change one key behavior: whether to climb, whether to walk away, whether to enter water or whether to avoid a predator.

There is no single “zombie switch.” Behavior emerges from communication between the nervous system, muscles and other tissues throughout the body. Different parasites have evolved different ways to interfere with those systems.

So biology cannot create the dancing dead of “Thriller” or the infected humans of “The Last of Us.” But if a zombie is a living organism whose normal behavior has been redirected by another organism, nature has already created plenty of them.
Studying these real-life zombies may help scientists understand not only how parasites manipulate their hosts, but also how normal behavior is generated and controlled in the first place.
Tara Deans receives funding from the National Institutes of Health.

articles.title: NASA Releases MAX POWER Key Events for Media, Participants
articles.dek: AmAmerica’s newest aerospace expo and air show – MAX POWER – is fast approaching, and NASA has announced key events beginning Friday, Nov.
paragraphs: AmAmerica’s newest aerospace expo and air show – MAX POWER – is fast approaching, and NASA has announced key events beginning Friday, Nov. 6, and running through Sunday, Nov. 8, hosted on and near the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Through multiple park experiences at MAX POWER , NASA and a variety of external collaborators will showcase the newest aircraft, autonomous vehicles, technologies, and more defining the future of air and space. NASA will display its quiet supersonic X-59 plane, and agency partners will showcase Moon rovers, spacecraft, and more. The expo also is a culmination of the agency’s recent Inspiration Tour , which included numerous flyovers to highlight NASA’s fleet of aircraft.
A current schedule of events is available on the agency’s website .

MAX POWER includes opportunities to meet leadership, astronauts, engineers, scientists, and other subject matter experts during the family-friendly public events with gates opening at 9 a. m. EST on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8.

NASA also will share multiple news updates during the weekend, including hosting a news conference at 5 p. m. on Nov. 7, to provide its latest Moon Base update. Located near the lunar South Pole, the Moon Base is humanity’s first outpost for long-term lunar exploration.
Live coverage of the news conference will stream on a variety of platforms online. Learn where to watch:

Media credentialing for this event is closed. Media approved for this event must request interviews in advance. Space in the news conference is limited, and first come, first served. Media also may participate in the news conference virtually. To request call details or an interview, please contact Lauren Low in the NASA Headquarters newsroom at: lauren. e. low@nasa. gov .
A short list of key NASA activities during MAX POWER are listed below. All times are listed in Eastern Standard Time, and are subject to change.

articles.title: Scientists Unlock a 1,000-Year-Old Mystery Buried Inside Ancient Melon Seeds
articles.dek: Ancient DNA recovered from melon seeds at a medieval Chinese port is revealing surprising clues about the fruit’s origins and evolution.
paragraphs: Ancient DNA recovered from melon seeds at a medieval Chinese port is revealing surprising clues about the fruit’s origins and evolution.

Melons grown in medieval China may have looked and tasted very different from the sweet varieties enjoyed today. DNA recovered from ancient seeds suggests these fruits had light-green flesh, yellow skin, and genetic ties to South Asia. Their appearance may also have reflected the artistic tastes of China’s Song dynasty.

The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , come from seeds discovered at the Gugang port (Shuomen Gugang) in southeastern China. Excavations in 2024 uncovered shipwrecks, porcelain, and remains of imported fruits. Waterlogged sediments preserved plant DNA dating to the Song dynasty (circa 960-1279).

Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis, working with colleagues in Germany and the United Kingdom, identified the seeds as belonging to the East Asian agrestis melon lineage. Genetic evidence suggests these melons originated in South Asia before reaching China, although independent domestication in China remains possible.

WashU biologist Susanne Renner, who has studied melons for more than 25 years, explained that scientists once favored a different origin. “At that time, it was assumed that because the genus Cucumis , to which melons belong, has numerous wild African species, that melons originated in Africa,” she said.

In 2010, Renner analyzed approximately 100 Cucumis samples from Africa, Australia, and Asia, identifying previously overlooked melon relatives around the Indian Ocean. “Based on biogeographic analysis, we inferred that melons most likely originated in Asia, not Africa,” Renner said. Research has since established separate domestication events in Northeast Africa and twice in India, with a possible additional event in southeastern China.

Two historical trade corridors could explain the arrival of South Asian melons in China. One followed the northern Silk Road along the Tibetan Plateau, while the other traveled south of the Himalayas through routes associated with the Tea Horse Road.

“Both corridors are historically plausible, as demonstrated by the movement of other food resources,” said WashU archaeologist Xinyi Liu. “Current archaeological evidence points more strongly to a southern route. The earliest melon remains in China have been recovered from Han and pre-Han royal tombs in southern China, predating comparable finds from northern ‘Silk Road’ sites by approximately 800 to 1,000 years. We therefore consider a southern route connecting southern China with Southeast and South Asia to be a candidate for the early introduction of melon into China.”

Genetic analysis suggests that melons cultivated during the 10th to 13th centuries had characteristics unlike those of modern dessert varieties. Rather than being selected primarily for sweetness, they may have been valued as vegetables, mildly sweet fruits, or sources of edible seeds.

“The color-related traits are particularly interesting. They suggest that these ancient melons likely had light-green flesh and yellow peel,” Liu said. “Melons with these characteristics are often consumed as vegetables, as mildly sweet fruit, or for their seeds, rather than as high-sugar dessert melons. In the lower Yangtze region today, culinary traditions of consuming melon as pickles or vegetables still persist.”

The fruit also held cultural meaning. Because melons contain numerous seeds, they traditionally symbolized fertility and prosperity in China. Their pale-green flesh may have complemented the aesthetic preferences of Song dynasty society.

Song dynasty artisans produced celadon pottery with delicate green glazes resembling jade. Many vessels were shaped like melons, suggesting a possible relationship between the fruit’s appearance and contemporary decorative traditions.

“The light-green color resonates with the fine-toned color of Chinese jade and with the glazes of celadon porcelain, both highly valued in East Asian aesthetic traditions,” Liu said. “During the Song dynasty, green celadon ceramics produced in the lower Yangtze region and beyond were frequently fashioned in melon-shaped forms , with glazes echoing the jade-green tones of melon flesh .”

Celadon ceramics circulated throughout China, Korea, and Japan, and numerous examples were recovered from Gugang. The researchers suggest that agricultural selection and cultural preferences may have influenced one another, although a direct connection remains unproven.

articles.title: Scientists Create Stunning, Car-Quality Paint Without Using a Single Pigment
articles.dek: A glossy, car-quality finish no longer has to depend on pigments.
paragraphs: A glossy, car-quality finish no longer has to depend on pigments. Researchers at Kobe University have developed a coating made from silicon nanoparticles that produces vivid, lasting color without the fading or angle-dependent shifts associated with many conventional coloring technologies.

Reported in the journal Small Structures , the advance combines several properties that have been difficult to achieve together: adjustable gloss, consistent color across viewing angles, compatibility with protective coatings, and application to large, three-dimensional surfaces. The technology could also dramatically reduce the weight of painted objects, including aircraft.

Traditional paints rely on pigments to absorb certain wavelengths of light and reflect others. These coatings often require relatively thick layers that add weight, while some pigments gradually degrade with exposure to sunlight. Structural color works differently. It arises from interactions between light and microscopic structures, as seen in the brilliant feathers of peacocks. However, reproducing these effects in manufactured coatings has generally required precisely arranged structures that can change appearance with viewing angle.

“Color coatings are expected to provide vivid color, brightness, gloss, and long-term durability, yet no existing technology satisfies all of these requirements simultaneously,” says Kobe University materials engineer Hiroshi Sugimoto. His earlier research established that silicon nanospheres could produce structural colors without unwanted viewing-angle shifts. His team subsequently developed an inkjet printing method for the material, but the resulting surfaces scattered light too diffusely to achieve a polished, glossy appearance.

The researchers addressed this limitation by surrounding silicon nanospheres with thin silica shells. These shells protect the particles and control the distance between them, encouraging more orderly arrangements that reduce diffuse light scattering. The improved organization makes it possible to produce a glossy finish while controlling its intensity.
“Packing the nano spheres in silica shells not only protects the particles but also controls their spacing and should improve self-assembly into neat arrays,” Sugimoto explains.

The team demonstrated the coating on large, complex three-dimensional surfaces and showed that an additional protective layer did not significantly alter the resulting color. This overcomes a major limitation of previous structural color systems, whose optical properties can be disrupted by protective coatings.

“The most exciting aspect of this work is that it demonstrates glossy, non-iridescent and protection-coated structural color coatings for 3D objects in a single platform, making the technology useful for real-world applications,” Sugimoto says.

The coating achieves high opacity and brightness using only a single layer of silicon nanospheres. This extremely thin structure offers a potentially enormous weight advantage over conventional paints. Coatings on wide-body passenger aircraft can add several hundred kilograms (about 660 pounds for 300 kilograms), whereas the researchers estimate that an equivalent structural color layer could theoretically weigh just several hundred grams (about 11 ounces for 300 grams). That comparison remains hypothetical rather than a demonstrated aircraft application.

The materials also offer potential environmental advantages. Silicon can be sourced from the semiconductor industry, while silica is among the most abundant materials in Earth’s crust. Because structural color does not depend on organic pigments that can break down under light exposure, the coatings could reduce fading and the need for replacement. Their actual environmental benefits at industrial scale have yet to be established.

Sugimoto is helping establish a company to bring the technology toward industrial production. The fabrication process can accommodate several established manufacturing techniques, potentially allowing the coatings to be applied over much larger areas.
“The process is compatible with scalable coating methods such as spray coating, slot-die coating, and roll-to-roll processing,” Sugimoto explains.

The research group’s longer-term ambitions extend beyond decorative and protective finishes. By engineering the optical behavior of silicon nanoparticles, the scientists hope to create coatings that perform additional functions, including detecting environmental changes, driving light-activated chemical reactions, and managing energy.

“We want to expand the possibility of applications for the science behind our technology beyond coloration. Looking ahead, we aim to develop multifunctional silicon nanoparticle coatings that combine structural coloration with additional optical functions such as sensing, photocatalysis, and energy management.”

articles.title: From 18th-century false ballots to the second JFK and double Dan Sullivans, a brief history of spoiler candidates and the unsuccessful legal challenges to them
articles.dek: Less than a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that people with links to Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s U. S.
paragraphs: Less than a week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that people with links to Alaska Democrat Mary Peltola’s U. S. Senate campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had recruited a candidate to the race whose name is nearly identical to that of the incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan, whom Peltola was challenging. The plan aimed to siphon votes from the incumbent senator and help Peltola win, according to the reporting.

The story has driven calls for prosecutions , lawsuits and state action . But as a political scientist who studies election law , I can say that the spoiler candidate is one of the oldest tricks in the American campaign toolbox, and the law has rarely touched it.
For most of the 1800s, American elections were conducted with ballots designed and printed by the parties. There were no official ballots printed by the state.

In those days, the addition of a rival name to a party ballot by an insidious printer could swing countless votes to the opposing party. The tactic was well known, and voters were often warned to look out for the “ Spurious Ticket .”
By the 1890s, the government-printed ballot had gained widespread adoption and ended the practice of counterfeit tickets. But that would not be enough to deter those who wanted to deceive voters.
As observers in Alaska have noted , recruiting candidates with similar or identical names is not a new move.

In John F. Kennedy’s first congressional primary, his opponent was a city councilor named Joseph Russo. An aide to Kennedy reportedly paid a janitor with the same name to enter the race. The real Russo complained, but in the end, Kennedy took more votes in the 1946 race than the Russos combined.

Eight years later, the name Kennedy worked the other way, when a Gillette stockroom supervisor named John Francis Kennedy , no relation, was elected as a Democrat to the position of treasurer and receiver-general of Massachusetts, owing in large part to the familiarity of his name. Names can move votes, so namesakes can be worth recruiting.
Some spoiler candidates are not necessarily meant to win votes. Sometimes they are there to amplify a message.

In 1978, Republican Carroll Campbell was running for an open House seat in upstate South Carolina. His opponent was Max Heller, the mayor of Greenville and a Jewish refugee from Nazi-occupied Austria.

Days before the election, Don Sprouse, an independent running for office for the first time, held a press conference and declared that Heller was unfit for office as he had “not made clear to the voters he is not a Christian” and was “not as qualified to represent the Christian people.”

Although Campbell condemned the remarks and Sprouse received only 1,693 votes, Heller lost the race. The allegations, still unproven, of Sprouse being a “stalking-horse” for Campbell only surfaced years later, but they continued to dog Campbell when he ran for governor in 1986.
Sprouse wasn’t going to spoil the election with the votes he could win, but he could be a spoiler with his message, an antisemitic appeal that Campbell would not make directly.
A different type of ballot shenanigan skips the recruitment and simply puts candidates on the ballot.

This was the case in 2010 when two Oakland County, Michigan, Democratic officials put candidates on the ballot under the Tea Party label in three races. The candidates didn’t even know they were running.
In this case, the law did come back to bite. The county party chair and operations director were charged with perjury and forgery , but the crime was forging signatures, not their strategy.

Some state election codes specifically discuss false declarations or forged election paperwork, but many don’t contemplate this type of scheme. Forgery and perjury, however, are illegal across the country, and it’s almost impossible to put an unwitting person on the ballot without one or the other.

In Alaska, this tactic can be used cheaply. There is no petition requirement to get on the ballot, just a $100 fee. Moreover, the parties can’t vet candidates in the primary. The state’s unique top-four primary system lets candidates choose their own party label.
The saga of Daniel J. Sullivan , the schoolteacher known as “Petersburg Sullivan” because of where he lives , and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan goes back longer than recent revelations.

Petersburg Sullivan filed to run as a Republican in the Senate race just three days before the deadline; state officials tried to bar him from the ballot. In June a judge said there was nothing in Alaska law to prevent him from appearing on the ballot, and the state Supreme Court subsequently agreed.

Since he couldn’t be removed, the state Division of Elections took unusual steps on their ballot design to help distinguish the two candidates. They listed Sen. Dan S. Sullivan as a Republican, marking him as the incumbent, and left Daniel J. Sullivan without a party designation . This had not been done for previous incumbents in at least a decade.

Assuming there is no forgery of documents with an unwitting and unwilling spoiler candidate, there is little the law can do. History shows us that the real legal exposure in these cases usually lies where it most often does in politics: money.

In a 2020 Miami, Florida, race, a former state senator turned political operative was convicted of three felonies related to efforts to recruit and pay a decoy candidate with the same surname as the Democratic incumbent. In another Florida case, a local Republican Party chair was convicted in connection with a scheme to plant a progressive alternative to siphon votes from the Democratic candidate. In both cases the prosecutions focused on campaign finance crimes, not simply on putting the spoilers on the ballot.

The state of Washington is an outlier, where it is a felony to run under a rival’s surname if the intent is to confuse voters . In 2024, two Bob Fergusons were recruited by conservative activist Glen Morgan to run for governor against state Attorney General Bob Ferguson. Both opted to drop out of their race under threat of prosecution.

articles.title: NASA Explores Potential Commercial Servicing for Hubble Telescope
articles.dek: NASA issued a Request for Information Oct. 29 to learn more about industry capabilities for in-space servicing to support the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope.
paragraphs: NASA issued a Request for Information Oct. 29 to learn more about industry capabilities for in-space servicing to support the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope.

“Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe.”

The Request for Information seeks commercial interest in: potentially conducting a mission to boost Hubble to a higher altitude to extend its science lifetime; servicing Hubble to enhance its capabilities; or performing a safe, controlled re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble’s mission.

“Hubble is a national icon that has fundamentally changed how humanity views our universe for more than 35 years,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing. Given the time we have until Hubble’s anticipated re-entry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow.”
The Request for Information is available online and will remain open for responses until 3 p. m. EST, Monday, Nov. 30.

Like all spacecraft in low Earth orbit, Hubble’s altitude is slowly decreasing over time because of atmospheric drag. Hubble does not have a propulsion system to maintain its own orbit, and analysis predicts Hubble is likely to re-enter the atmosphere in the 2033 to 2034 timeframe. As such, NASA anticipates that a mission would need to take place by 2032.

The Hubble Space Telescope has been operating for more than three decades and continues to make ground-breaking discoveries that shape our fundamental understanding of the universe. Hubble is a project of international cooperation between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency). NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, manages the telescope and mission operations. Lockheed Martin Space, based in Denver, also supports mission operations at Goddard. The Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, conducts Hubble science operations for NASA.

articles.title: New Treatment Strategy Makes Cancer Cells Run Out of Energy and Die
articles.dek: Researchers have discovered a way to kill leukemia cells by forcing them to remain highly active even as their energy supply is disrupted.
paragraphs: Researchers have discovered a way to kill leukemia cells by forcing them to remain highly active even as their energy supply is disrupted. The experimental treatment has produced promising results in mice and patient-derived cancer cells, including a particularly aggressive form of the disease that often resists treatment.

The approach targets acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a rapidly progressing cancer of the blood and bone marrow that interferes with normal blood cell production. Developed by researchers at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, the treatment exploits the energy demands of malignant cells rather than directly attacking their DNA.

At the center of the strategy is mTOR, a protein that helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and activity. Under normal conditions, cells adjust these processes according to their available resources. The researchers designed a molecule called AcTor that blocks a signaling protein involved in controlling mTOR, allowing growth signals to remain active even when cellular energy production is impaired.

AcTor was combined with ixazomib (IXZ), a drug used to inhibit cancer cell proliferation. Together, the treatments disrupt energy production in mitochondria while preventing leukemia cells from slowing their activity. Unable to balance their energy needs with their available resources, the cancer cells experience severe stress and die.
The treatment emerged from a collaboration between biochemist Boaz Tirosh and computational chemist Leif Eriksson, whose expertise helped turn the underlying hypothesis into a potential drug.

“Boaz Tirosh is a biochemist and understands the processes taking place within a cell. It was he who put forward the hypothesis for this treatment. I am a computational chemist and have designed a molecule that enters the cancerous cell and alters it in the way we want,” says Leif Eriksson, Professor of Physical Chemistry at the University of Gothenburg.

In a study published in Molecular Cancer , the combination of AcTor and ixazomib demonstrated strong activity against AML in laboratory cell lines, primary samples from patients, and animal experiments. It also remained effective against TP53-mutant AML, an especially aggressive form of leukemia associated with poor outcomes and limited treatment options.

The researchers found that the treatment eliminated malignant blood cells as well as leukemic stem cells. These stem cells can survive conventional therapies and regenerate the disease, contributing to relapse. The mouse experiments also suggested that the treatment could avoid the development of drug resistance, although this has not been established in patients.
“It’s a completely new method and does not affect healthy blood cells; furthermore, our studies in mice show that drug resistance is avoided, which can otherwise happen,” says Leif Eriksson.

The researchers also detected a biological response that might eventually help doctors assess whether the treatment is working. Cells exposed to the drug combination released a protein called ADM2, which could potentially serve as a measurable indicator of treatment activity.

“We also observed that our treatment triggered the release of a protein (ADM2), which could therefore serve as a biomarker for the treatment’s response. This could guide future translational and clinical studies,” says Leif Eriksson.

The findings remain preclinical, meaning that the combination has not yet been shown to be safe or effective in humans. Further studies will be needed to confirm its activity, evaluate potential side effects, and determine whether it can progress to clinical trials. Patients with relapsed or refractory AML, whose disease has returned or failed to respond to treatment, could be among those who might benefit if the approach eventually proves successful.
Instead of relying primarily on treatments that damage cancer cell DNA, the research focuses on disrupting the metabolic processes that allow leukemia cells to survive.

“Our study is an example of the shift toward focusing research on cancer metabolism within cells, rather than relying solely on methods that damage DNA. Drug development is very expensive, but we hope that our findings will generate sufficient interest to enable us to continue our research into a cure for this serious disease,” says Leif Eriksson.

articles.title: A Promising Way To Reverse Cognitive Decline Just Failed a Major Clinical Test
articles.dek: Restoring blood flow to the brain seemed a promising way to protect thinking skills, but opening severely narrowed arteries did not deliver the cognitive boost researchers…
paragraphs: Restoring blood flow to the brain seemed a promising way to protect thinking skills, but opening severely narrowed arteries did not deliver the cognitive boost researchers hoped for.

A Columbia -led randomized trial found that people with severe carotid artery narrowing gained no additional cognitive benefit from stenting or surgery compared with medication alone over one year. The findings challenge the idea that reopening these arteries can reverse cognitive decline in patients without associated symptoms.

“We had hoped that improving blood flow in the brain in this way would improve cognition—and there were tantalizing clues from animal studies and case series that it would,” says study leader Randolph Marshall, MD, the Elisabeth K. Harris Professor of Neurology at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons. “But when we put it to the test in a randomized clinical trial, comparing cognition after opening the blockage or treatment with medication alone, we did not see a difference.”

The carotid arteries run through the neck and supply blood to the brain. Severe narrowing, known as carotid stenosis, is associated with cognitive impairment even in people who have never had a stroke. The link is particularly apparent when blood flow to the brain is reduced.

That connection raised a compelling possibility: restoring circulation might help preserve or improve cognition. Stenting holds a narrowed artery open, while surgery removes the material causing the blockage.

“We’ve thought for a long time that improving cognition by restoring blood flow with stenting or surgery could improve cognition, but until our study, the hypothesis had never been tested in a randomized clinical trial.”

To investigate, the researchers enrolled 291 patients in CREST-H, all with carotid artery narrowing of at least 70% but no associated symptoms. They assessed brain blood flow and cognition at enrollment and again one year later. Cognitive scores improved slightly in both groups, but patients who underwent a procedure did no better than those treated with medication alone.

CREST-H was part of CREST-2, a larger multicenter trial that Marshall helped design to compare approaches to preventing strokes in people with severe carotid blockages. In that trial, adding stenting to medication cut strokes by about half compared with medication alone. Surgery to remove the blockage did not show the same benefit.

“Those results do appear to have changed practice already, and more of these patients are getting stents,” says Marshall. The cognitive findings, however, suggest that patients should not expect the procedure to improve their thinking skills beyond what medication alone provides.

“We concluded that revascularization to reverse cognitive decline in these patients cannot be expected. Therefore, we need to reinforce the importance of preventing carotid stenosis to avoid its consequences,” says Marshall.

This study is supported by the NIH (R01NS097876). The CREST-2 parent trials are supported by the NIH (U01NS080168, U01NS080165, and U01NS086872), the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, and the Department of Health and Human Services.
